### Portuguese domination
[edit]
Mombasa was under Portuguese rule from 1593 to 1698 and again from 1728 to 1729. Portuguese presence in Kenya lasted from 1498 until 1730.
Vasco da Gama was the first known European to visit Mombasa, receiving a chilly reception in 1498.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mombasa#cite_note-15) Two years later, the town was sacked by the Portuguese. In 1502, the sultanate became independent from Kilwa Kisiwani and was renamed as Mvita (in Swahili) or Manbasa (Arabic).
The Portuguese had since had encounters with the city several times; first under Francisco de Almeida in 1505, later under Afonso de Albuquerque in 1522 to quell an attempted mutiny by the sultan's nephew in Pemba and Zanzibar, and finally the destruction of the city under Nuno da Cunha again in 1528 after the Malindi sultan failed to pay tribute.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mombasa#cite_note-:02-16)
In 1585, a military expedition of the Ottoman Empire, led by Emir 'Ali Bey, successfully captured Mombasa, and other coastal cities in Southeast Africa from the Portuguese.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mombasa#cite_note-17) However, Malindi remained loyal to Portugal. The Zimba overcame the towns of Sena and Tete on the Zambezi, and in 1587 they took Kilwa, killing 3,000 people. At Mombasa, the Zimba slaughtered the Muslim inhabitants, but they were halted at Malindi by the Bantu-speaking Segeju and went home. This stimulated the Portuguese to take over Mombasa a third time in 1589, and four years later they built Fort Jesus to administer the region. Between Lake Malawi and the Zambezi mouth, Kalonga Mzura made an alliance with the Portuguese in 1608 and fielded 4,000 warriors to help defeat their rival Zimba, who were led by chief Lundi._[citation needed_]
texts.7:
### Portuguese domination
After the building of Fort Jesus, Mombasa was put by the Portuguese under the rule of members of the ruling family of Malindi. In 1631 Dom Jeronimo, the ruler of Mombasa, slaughtered the Portuguese garrison in the city and defeated the relief force sent by the Portuguese. In 1632 Dom Jeronimo left Mombasa and became a pirate. That year the Portuguese returned and established direct rule over Mombasa.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mombasa#cite_note-18)
With the capture of Fort Jesus in 1698, the town came under the influence of the Imamate of Oman, subordinate to the Omani rulers on the island of Unguja, prompting regular local rebellions. Oman appointed three consecutive Governors (Wali in Arabic, Liwali in Swahili):
*   12 December 1698 – December 1698: Imam Sa'if ibn Sultan  
*   December 1698 – 1728: Nasr ibn Abdallah al-Mazru'i  
*   1728–12 March 1728: Shaykh Rumba
Mombasa was briefly returned to Portuguese rule by captain-major Álvaro Caetano de Melo Castro (12 March 1728 – 21 September 1729), then four new Omani Liwali until 1746, when the last of them made it independent again (disputed by Oman), as the first of its recorded Sultans:

The 500-year-old Portuguese cross that marks a turning point in world history
Standing on a coral promontory at the southern end of Malindi Bay, this whitewashed pillar topped with a cross was erected by Vasco da Gama in 1498 — one of the oldest European monuments in sub-Saharan Africa.

## About Vasco da Gama Pillar
The Vasco da Gama Pillar is a padrão a coral-stone navigation pillar the Portuguese planted along the African and Indian coasts to mark their claim of new territories. Erected in 1498 as da Gama sailed to India, this pillar in Malindi is the only original padrão still standing on its original site in East Africa. The Sultan of Malindi received da Gama warmly (unlike the hostile welcome he had received in Mombasa) and even provided the Indian navigator Ahmed ibn Majid, whose knowledge of the monsoon winds guided the Portuguese fleet across the Arabian Sea to Calicut. This meeting effectively opened the sea route between Europe and Asia. The pillar’s stark white silhouette against the turquoise ocean is one of Malindi’s iconic images. It stands on a coral outcrop that becomes a small island at high tide, ringed by rock pools that reveal starfish, sea urchins, and darting reef fish. Nearby, the small Portuguese Chapel, one of the oldest Christian buildings in East Africa, is often visited alongside the pillar as part of a compact heritage circuit.

_by Ian Packham_
I was on the Kenyan coast at Malindi, having followed the African coast west from Tangier, Morocco’s seedy port of entrance for so many Europeans. The 500-year-old Portuguese cross that marks a turning point in world history

## About Vasco da Gama Pillar
The Vasco da Gama Pillar is a padrão a coral-stone navigation pillar the Portuguese planted along the African and Indian coasts to mark their claim of new territories. Erected in 1498 as da Gama sailed to India, this pillar in Malindi is the only original padrão still standing on its original site in East Africa. The Sultan of Malindi received da Gama warmly (unlike the hostile welcome he had received in Mombasa) and even provided the Indian navigator Ahmed ibn Majid, whose knowledge of the monsoon winds guided the Portuguese fleet across the Arabian Sea to Calicut. This meeting effectively opened the sea route between Europe and Asia. The pillar’s stark white silhouette against the turquoise ocean is one of Malindi’s iconic images. It stands on a coral outcrop that becomes a small island at high tide, ringed by rock pools that reveal starfish, sea urchins, and darting reef fish. Nearby, the small Portuguese Chapel, one of the oldest Christian buildings in East Africa, is often visited alongside the pillar as part of a compact heritage circuit.

## Vasco da Gama Pillar
### What to expect
The Vasco da Gama Pillar is a historic monument in Malindi, not Mombasa, and it is one of the oldest surviving European monuments on the East African coast. It was originally associated with Portuguese explorer Vasco da Gama’s return voyage in 1499, and the pillar today stands as a coastal landmark overlooking the Indian Ocean. The pillar is a stone **padrão** topped with a cross, and the National Museums of Kenya says it is the only known original padrão from the Portuguese coastal explorations. It was declared a gazetted national monument in 1935 and is now managed under the National Museums of Kenya. Historically, the pillar is tied to early Portuguese navigation and trade along the East African coast. It also reflects the relationship between Portuguese sailors and the rulers of Malindi at the time. For many visitors, it is less about the monument alone and more about the sea views and the sense of standing at a place linked to the Age of Exploration.

The fortified outposts of sub-Saharan West Africa were integral to Europe’s expansion into the non-Western World during the second half of the fifteenth century and they remain icons of the Atlantic trade. The early forts, built in the late fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, are associated with the Portuguese attempt to monopolize West African commerce. Collectively they initiated lasting transformations in the political economies and cultural traditions of the African societies with which they interacted. This chapter considers the historical context in which the forts were established, their structural histories, and current condition.

**Malindi Museum** is a museum located in Malindi, Kenya. It has control over four main heritage sites: The Vasco da Gama Pillar, The Portuguese Chapel, The House of Columns and The Heritage Complex museum.

In 1991 the Malindi Museum Society was formed to support the policy of the National Museums of Kenya to acquire a historic building in Malindi that could be turned into a museum.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-2) Malindi's first museum building was opened in 2004, located in a two story building dating from 1891 known as The House of Columns. The building was constructed by Adulhussein Gulamhussein.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-3) The Bohra community sold the building for 2,000 English pounds.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-NMK-4) The building operated as an Indian trading center since its establishment in 1891.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-:0-5) The building that houses the museum was used as Malindi's first native hospital.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-6) On the east facade there is a colonnade featuring five round pillars. The building served as a hospital and headquarters of the Department of Fisheries.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-7) In 1991, it was declared a national monument.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-8) In 1999 the House of Columns was transferred to the National Museum of Kenya and a restoration opened in 2004 as museum.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-NMK-4)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-Martin1970-9)

In 2013 Malindi Museum acquired a second set of buildings: the former offices of the District Commissioner, about 300 metres northwest along Silversand Road. This is now known as Malindi Museum Heritage Complex, the main building of which houses the ethnographic collections.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-10) Malindi Museum also has responsibility for two other heritage sites in the town: The Vasco da Gama Pillar and The Portuguese Chapel.
Coelacanth in The House of Columns
The Heritage Complex museum contains various historical artefacts from Malindi.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-11) The museum has exhibits containing traditional objects such as musical instruments, tools and costumes. On the ethnographic section, the museum contains various artefacts of the Mijikenda peoples who are ethnic groups inhabiting the Kenyan coast, including wooden totems,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-:0-5) as well as ancient artifacts that belonged to Arabs who settled in Malindi.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-12) In addition, the museum features artefacts from other communities that inhabit the Kenyan coast, as well as objects from the Swahili civilization.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-13) The museum features exhibits about fish species and the history of Malindi.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-14)

The House of Columns features temporary exhibits including famous _Malindi Coelacanth_.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-NMK-4)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-Martin1970-9) The museum also contains artifacts related to the explorer Vasco da Gama.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-15)The House of Columns has exhibits from the Portuguese period of Kenya's coastal zone, as well as photographs of some of the country's archeological sites.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-16) In addition, the museum owns the Webb Memorial Library which has books on the history and culture of the Kenyan coast.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-17)
A single ticket currently (2023) covers the four sites under the control of Malindi Museum. These are: The Vasco da Gama Pillar, The Portuguese Chapel, The House of Columns and the Malindi Museum Heritage Complex.

### Malindi Museum Day Tour - Old Town | Vasco da Gama Pillar & Portuguese Chapel
**Our Malindi Museum Day tour** combines a visit to the Malindi Museum, a stroll through **Malindi’s old town**, a visit to **Vasco da Gama’s pillar**, and the **Portuguese chapel**.
The Museum is located east of Malindi town, next to Uhuru Gardens, along the seafront, and a few meters from Malindi jetty and Fish Market.
The museum also serves as an information center, where visitors can find more information about attractions and events in Malindi. You also get to visit the famous Vasco da Gama Pillar, which was erected by the Portuguese explorer **Vasco da Gama** as a navigational aid in 1498.
The coral column, topped with a cross of Lisbon stone, is one of the most popular landmarks on the Kenyan Coast.
The other attraction you will visit, the Portuguese Chapel, was also built by Vasco da Gama and is the first Christian place of worship in East Africa.

#### **Morning: Historical Circuit**

## Popular Malindi Attractions
Malindi Museum
**One of Malindi's popular attractions, the Malindi Museum, is also the Tourism Information Centre for the town of Malindi in Kenya.**
The Malindi museum is unsure of the actual date that the building that it is housed in was constructed, but they think it was built towards the end of the 19th century as it is built in the typical style fashionable during this era, especially in the old towns of Lamu and Mombasa.
The building, known as the column house, is a charming, double storey structure, with a tiled roof, located a few metres from the Malindi jetty and fish market. The building has served many functions in the past; it has acted as a Native Civil hospital until 1952 and then as the Malindi Fisheries Office.
Until it was finally handed over to the National Museums of Kenya in 1999. In May 2004 the building opened its doors to the general public as Malindi Museum.
The building has four entrances. Two on the east facade are reached through a colonnade of 5 rounded pillars. One entrance has an Indian Gujerati 9 hand fitted to it, the other with a Swahili carved door. The third entrance is on the northern facade up a masonry stairway, it has a small trap door of Indian type serving both the ground and first floor of the building.
The fourth entrance, exclusively for the first floor, is on the southern facade is reached via an external wooden staircase. The door to this entrance is simple but opens onto a balcony. Inside on the first floor, there are examples of beautifully carved Bajuni doors. The museum currently houses temporary exhibitions.
For an interesting way to spend a half day, and gain a better understanding of the history of Malindi you can visit the following places; which are close to each other: Vasco da Gama pillar, Portuguese Chapel and the Malindi Museum (also known as the Column House). You can use the same ticket purchased for entrance to the Museum to enter all three places.

This is now known as Malindi Museum Heritage Complex, the main building of which houses the ethnographic collections.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-10) Malindi Museum also has responsibility for two other heritage sites in the town: The Vasco da Gama Pillar and The Portuguese Chapel.
Coelacanth in The House of Columns
The Heritage Complex museum contains various historical artefacts from Malindi.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-11) The museum has exhibits containing traditional objects such as musical instruments, tools and costumes. On the ethnographic section, the museum contains various artefacts of the Mijikenda peoples who are ethnic groups inhabiting the Kenyan coast, including wooden totems,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-:0-5) as well as ancient artifacts that belonged to Arabs who settled in Malindi.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-12) In addition, the museum features artefacts from other communities that inhabit the Kenyan coast, as well as objects from the Swahili civilization.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-13) The museum features exhibits about fish species and the history of Malindi.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-14)

The House of Columns features temporary exhibits including famous _Malindi Coelacanth_.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-NMK-4)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-Martin1970-9) The museum also contains artifacts related to the explorer Vasco da Gama.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-15)The House of Columns has exhibits from the Portuguese period of Kenya's coastal zone, as well as photographs of some of the country's archeological sites.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-16) In addition, the museum owns the Webb Memorial Library which has books on the history and culture of the Kenyan coast.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi_Museum#cite_note-17)
A single ticket currently (2023) covers the four sites under the control of Malindi Museum. These are: The Vasco da Gama Pillar, The Portuguese Chapel, The House of Columns and the Malindi Museum Heritage Complex.

**The Vasco Da Gama Pillar**
The 15th Century was an era of worldwide exploration by Portugal. Early in the Century, Portugal had conceived an idea of commemorating visits of Portuguese vessels in different domains. In 1497, King Dom Manuel of Portugal appointed Vasco da Gama to command a fleet of 4 ships to sail to India through the Far East. The Fleet left Portugal on the 8th of July, 1497 and after many adventures, anchored off Malindi on Easter Sunday 15th April, 1498. Read More…
**The Portuguese Chapel**
The Portuguese presence in Malindi began with the arrival of Vasco da Gama in 1498. On his second voyage to India, he left a group of solders in Malindi and a Chapel built in the style of that of the Navigator`s at Sagres in Portugal and a Portuguese` factory ‘or trading base which included store houses, barracks, residences and offices. **The House of Columns (Malindi Museum)**
Though the date of construction of this unique structure is not known, it is known that it was used by Adulhussein Gulamhussein & Co. There is photographic evidence of its existence in 1891 when W. Fitzgerald took a picture of it from on board the IBEA’s coasting steamer, the Henry Wright, the boat that took him up to the coast from Mombasa to Lamu during his survey of the agricultural potential of the Kenya Coast. **The Malindi Heritage Complex Museum**
This building was constructed in early 1890`s for the Imperial British East Africa Company ( IBEA Co.) which by British Royal Charter took over for 50 years the Sultan of Zanzibar`s mainland concession from Kipini to Vanga ( the coastal strip ). Mr. Bell Smith, an employee of IBEA Co., oversaw the construction of the building, known then as the District Collector`s Office, to serve as the company’s first office. Read More..
